title: The Aesthetics of Nothingness
text:
In The Aesthetics of Nothingness, Sara Aliscioni explores emptiness, loneliness and absence through a series of photographs that observe ordinary situations from an estranging, sometimes ironic and paradoxical perspective. Anonymous spaces, isolated figures and everyday scenes become the subjects of images in which action seems suspended and every presence appears to be waiting for something that may never arrive. The project draws conceptual inspiration from Samuel Beckett’s Waiting for Godot, in which waiting becomes an existential condition and the absence of a decisive event is an integral part of the narrative. This dimension is translated into photography through static situations, inconclusive gestures and figures that seem unable to find a precise place in the world. The result is a representation of nothingness that retains a sarcastic edge, exposing the absurdity of certain behaviours and rituals of everyday life.

Among the project’s visual references is the cinema of Roy Andersson, particularly his frontal staging, static compositions and dry humour, which coexists with melancholy. As in the Swedish director’s films, everyday life in these photographs takes on a theatrical dimension, poised between realism and absurdity.

The project is also distinguished by a deliberate formal choice: the use of colour, in contrast with the artist’s customary black-and-white practice. This is not simply a technical variation, but an aesthetic decision integral to the work. Colour helps define the settings, emphasise their artificiality and bring out the ordinary, sometimes impersonal character of the situations depicted. The hues become part of the image-making process, helping to create a distance between what is seen and what is perceived.

The Aesthetics of Nothingness thus offers a visual reflection on inaction, waiting and the difficulty of assigning meaning to events. Through carefully constructed images marked by a subtle sense of irony, Sara Aliscioni transforms emptiness into a photographic subject, portraying a world in which even absence can become visible.

title: Meta Est
text:
### Introduction

Meta-East is a visual journey through the suspended territories of Eastern Europe and beyond, told through the power of black and white—not as an aesthetic choice, but as the existential condition of these places. Not out of nostalgia, but out of necessity. Color deceives. It lies. Only shadow and shades of grey can truly tell the story. Venturing into the dark heart of the East, where reality dissolves into symbols and borders become porous, a silent world emerges: motionless, inhabited by enigmatic presences, faces outside of time, bodies shaped by labor, endurance, and disorientation.

Every image is a riddle, an interrupted gesture, a question left unanswered. This portfolio crosses both geographical and inner frontiers, exploring countries where time appears to have stalled, suspended in an endless present built upon contradiction and paradox. Yet Meta-East is not merely a geographical direction. It is a state of mind, an inner landscape dense with symbols, rituals, absences, and apparitions. It is an aesthetic of waiting, an emotional geography where the East ceases to be a place and becomes an existential condition.

Here we encounter men and women whose faces have been carved by history, whose gazes speak of faith, identity, and resilience. Religions coexist—or merely brush against one another—in silence, offering no consolation. Cities sway between their Soviet past and an uncertain present. Rural landscapes remain untouched by the promises of modernity, where progress arrives only as a distant echo. Roads no longer lead anywhere; they become labyrinths. Each photograph opens a breach into a reality that feels at once metaphysical and surreal, yet profoundly tangible.

Ghost towns drift past weathered churches, bare rooms cut by sharp light. Men and women appear as though they have stepped out of a frozen dream—or from a nightmare that never fully awakened. Everything is real, yet nothing feels entirely so, like still frames depicting the architecture of the mind. Meta-East does not seek to show; it seeks to question. It does not explain; it unsettles. It is a diary of apparitions, of marginal lives, fractured identities, saints and madmen. A theatre of human absurdity, where the East is no longer a direction but an open wound.

It is a slow passage, undertaken with open eyes and a suspended heart, across territories where time no longer flows but settles into deep folds, like dust gathering in the cracks of ancient icons. It is a silent hymn suspended between East and West, between the visible and the invisible, between those who remain and those who dream of leaving. The faces speak with the gravity of those who have watched centuries pass without ever departing.

Religions whisper through folded hands and shadows lingering on thresholds. Society appears fragmented, yet mysteriously held together by a luminous melancholy. Here, absurdity is not a scream but a restrained breath. Every photograph is an unfinished sentence, a thought dissolving into mist and onion domes, slow footsteps and dense silence. The landscape is never a backdrop—it is consciousness itself. The land becomes memory; the road becomes flow. Even the smallest gesture seems charged with an ancient significance, as though unfolding within a vision already telling its own story. Meta-East portrays an inner expanse, a marginal yet profoundly human world caught within its own eternal return. This is not a journey toward somewhere else. It is a journey inward, where poetry and reality walk hand in hand like two sisters who bear little resemblance, yet understand one another perfectly.

Meta-East is a line, a threshold—perhaps a wound. Countries without an hour, where time sleeps beneath asphalt and asbestos. Faces that look without asking. Things that happen slowly, or perhaps have already happened. A low sky. Milky light. Twisting roads. Houses waiting for no one. This is not the East. It is what the East becomes when you look at it for too long.

It is not a place to visit, but one to inhabit with your gaze. Every photograph is a fragment, a whisper, a room from a childhood never remembered. Meta-East is not a point on the map. It is an elsewhere that walks beside you, living inside the dreams you never dreamed and the words that never came. It is what remains when the search comes to an end: a silent extension of the soul, where everything is still while everything moves within. An inner atlas of Europe’s forgotten landscapes, where the East is no longer an orientation but a condition: territories suspended between the visible and the invisible, history and stillness, humanity and archetype.

### Synopsis

Meta-East is a visual inquiry into the margins of Eastern Europe, filtering everyday life through a gaze suspended between documentary observation and poetic abstraction. The project unfolds through a series of portraits, landscapes, and narrative sequences that move along symbolic borders—geographical, temporal, and psychological—exploring the condition of the unseen: bodies, gazes, and objects inhabiting marginal worlds, distant from dominant narratives.

Meta-East seeks to bring to the surface the subterranean presence of these micro-civilizations, revealing their fragile dignity and the tension between visibility and disappearance, memory and oblivion. Sara Aliscioni approaches questions of identity, resistance, ritual, and solitude without resorting to overt denunciation. Instead, she works through the evocative power of images, the use of natural light, and a close attention to unexpected forms. The work asks how the gaze—whether human or mechanical—contributes to bringing what it observes into being, or consigning it to the shadows.

Her images oscillate between visual elegy and radical minimalism: unsettled surfaces, oblique light, theatrical spaces either empty or inhabited by precarious figures, as though time itself had been suspended. Meta-East inhabits a contemporary landscape of hybrid aesthetics, somewhere between documentary photography and conceptual experimentation, reflecting on the contradictions that shape Eastern Europe: the memory of the Soviet past, migration, marginality, and social transformation.

Yet Aliscioni rejects both charitable rhetoric and the picturesque gaze. Instead, she entrusts the images with a slow, accumulated power—the subtle magic of spaces that have been denied visibility, and the quiet resilience of those who remain unseen.

title: The Tailors
text:
The series The Tailors stems from my personal photographic exploration of traditional trades in Casablanca, the largest city in Morocco.

Immortalized by the cult film of the same name, the country’s economic capital is the ultimate business destination.

Using petit taxis as my means of transport—old red cars driven by private drivers who often did not know the destination and would lose their way among unfamiliar streets—I explored both central and outlying neighborhoods, photographing different categories of artisans as well as the most popular markets. In the heart of the non-touristic Medina, my subjects included butchers and sellers of fabrics, spices and dates.

Artisans and shopkeepers would interrupt their activities during the Islamic prayer, salat, a prescribed and obligatory ritual. During this time, I observed their practices within the setting of a city that seemed suspended in time, enveloped in the muffled sound of litanies intended to reassure the faithful.

Documenting these trades presented many challenges.

Photography in Morocco is extremely difficult: people regard not only travelers, but especially cameras, with suspicion.

This attitude stems from popular beliefs that remain deeply rooted in the culture, according to which a portrait can steal a person’s soul. Photography is therefore perceived as a spell, a form of magic that traps the soul inside the photographic print.

I chose to document, through rigorously black-and-white images, a group of tailors working for a renowned boutique in the country’s commercial capital, the beating heart of its economy.

Looking out of the window of the building hosting one of the main exhibitions of the International Festival of Arts and Migration in the Metaverse, held every November, I noticed a tailoring workshop in one of the apartments across the street.

I was immediately struck by the silhouettes moving silently, almost as if performing the choreography of a black-and-white silent film.

I asked one of the festival organizers if they could help me meet, get to know and photograph the workshop’s workers. After three days, I finally managed to enter the tailoring workshop, where a scene suspended between dream and reality unfolded before me.

Being a tailor has always required skill and expertise, as well as patience and passion. Designing, altering, repairing, sewing and making garments are just some of the tasks tailors must be able to perform throughout their working day.

Young apprentices, as well as older men with many years of experience, all wear the indispensable measuring tape around their necks. Through dedication, patience and repeated gestures, these invisible tailors create garments for Casablanca’s elite and for the King himself, a source of pride for each of them.

The faces of women and men appear within frames shaped by the very spaces in which they work, surrounded by fabrics, scissors, bobbins, ironing boards, dress forms and sewing machines.

The men, curious yet skeptical, and the women, shy but also carrying the concealed enthusiasm of those chosen to pose as models, placed their trust in me and my camera, moving beyond the beliefs that Moroccan society continues to hold on to.

Human figures blend with the silhouettes of mannequins, moving across a stage that seems to belong to a world from another era. In silence and through harmonious movements, the tailors become true artists, creating garments that the upper classes wear and display with elegance and pride.

They became the protagonists of my project, the chosen subjects of my portraits, captured in images that would make them immortal.

Portraiture has always played a crucial role in photography, which, despite its evolution, has never ceased to be associated with the representation of people.

Walter Benjamin wrote:

“For photography, renouncing the human figure is the most difficult thing of all.” And it is here that the authentic, subjective representation of these portraits takes shape: The Tailors.

title: NFT Artist Portraits
text:
That artistic and personal vision is crucial in the rendering of a portrait becomes evident when the crypto artists move within a context that refers to their artwork and are photographed.

The NFTs Artists portraits project was born from Sara Aliscioni's vision aimed at immortalizing the protagonists of the new international scene, explorers of the crypto world.

The photos portray the authors of the new art forms that involve the digitization of a physical work or the creation of a digital work.

Italian and international artists have posed in various places and contexts.

Rome, Milan, Venice, Turin, Pisa, Imperia, Latina and Casablanca are among the cities that have been the background to the portraits.

The photographic choice, with a strictly black and white calligraphy, proposes images built on the inspiration that the photographer has drawn from the knowledge of both the artists and their art. The portrait has always played a crucial role in photography which, despite its evolutions, has continued to be associated with the representation of people. Walter Benjamin wrote:

“The renunciation of the human figure is the most difficult of all things for photography”. In the twentieth century, with the explosion of Pop Art, Andy Warhol with his Self Portraits and with his portraits of characters such as Marilyn Monroe, Jean-Michel Basquiat and Man Ray, made the faces of these protagonists iconic giving the portraits a central aspect and well embedded in contemporary visual culture.

Within a refined setting composed in a very personal key, Sara offers a portfolio of photos of artists who have posed, portraying, through their image, themselves and their artistic language within a frame that refers to their own work.

The project therefore has as its main objective that of witnessing some of the precursors of the new frontier of interconnected virtual and real worlds, such as the NFTs, restoring that sort of immortality that man has always pursued.

The new exponents who are giving life to a new way of making art, Crypto Art, merging with their artistic vision reinterpreted by the photographer Sara Aliscioni, become witnesses of an unprecedented collection that comes from the desire to show, through the faces, the ways and attitudes, a new chapter of contemporary Art.

title: Human/Animal
endorsement: In her photographs, Sara Aliscioni reveals the complex relationship between humans and animals. One that is not easily translated into words, but exists through her images. The question of what separates the animal from the human pervades these provocative photographs.
text:
Human/Animal is a photographic project by Sara Aliscioni that explores the relationship between humans and animals without imposing a single reading or an explicitly critical stance.

The work resists the dimension of denunciation and instead occupies an unstable space, where what is observed is never fully fixed. The series emerges from a precise shift: not what this relationship represents, but how it is lived by those who undergo it and move through it without having chosen it. The animal is at the centre—not as a symbol, but as a presence.

The animals portrayed inhabit different conditions: they are cared for, confined, displayed, used. They can function as emotional refuge, projection, aesthetic element, or response to an inner void. In other cases, they exist within systems that determine their entire life cycle.

These conditions are not separated. They coexist.

Within these relationships, love also exists—real, concrete, everyday love. It appears in repeated gestures, in care, in constant proximity. In attention to the smallest details, in the recognition of the animal’s individuality. It is neither simulated nor accessory; it is an integral part of the bond. Yet it does not cancel the structure in which it is produced. From the animal’s perspective, the relationship is not a concept. It is a given. It recognizes a recurring presence: the one who feeds, who touches, who defines space. Their absence interrupts a rhythm; their presence restores it. This can produce a form of calm, of reassurance, but at the same time it builds a dependency that is not chosen.

The animal does not possess its own time and space: it moves within limits defined by others, gradually traversing them until they become familiar. Habit replaces possibility. It is not possible to determine whether there is adherence; what is evident is adaptation. Some behaviors may be read as affection, others as mere tolerance.

In both cases, the asymmetry remains intact: one party defines the conditions, the other accepts them. It is at this point that the relationship fractures: care does not oppose control —it contains it. Love does not eliminate possession; it passes through it. Protection implies a reduction of the field of existence, and closeness implies continuous dependency. What could be defined as the “Noah Syndrome”—the human need to protect, save, and hold onto—translates, on the animal’s side, into a condition from which no exit is foreseen. A form of permanence that can be read, without confirmation, as forced adaptation. A possible “Stockholm Syndrome” without declaration, without consciousness, without language. A question remains that cannot be verified: if the animal could choose, would it alter this condition? It is not known in which direction. In these portraits, the human figure does not dominate; it is present, but not central. The animal occupies the image with equal intensity, at times with greater force. In its gaze there is no request, nor any readable complicity. It does not confirm the relationship. It exposes it.

A minimal but persistent fracture emerges: the observer is included. The human defines itself as caretaker, as a necessary figure.

But it is also the one who establishes the ultimate boundary of the animal’s existence. This ambivalence is not stated, but remains implicit in every image. The project takes no position.

Photography intervenes as an act of arresting space and time, without altering the condition and without either releasing or confining. It removes these presences from immediate disappearance without changing their structure. It renders them visible for what they are: lives existing within a system that contains them.

A non-verifiable yet unavoidable possibility remains to be asked: if the animal could break away, would it? And if it did, would the human be willing not to prevent it?

The question cannot be resolved. And it is not resolved.
Sara Aliscioni

title: Last Sacrament
text:
Ultimo Sacramento a photographic body of work that wanders through the residual traces of religion embedded in the fabric of contemporary urban life.

It draws from the raw gaze of Diane Arbus, the existential stillness of Béla Tarr, and the stark symbolism of Ingmar Bergman, moving through portraits, street scenes, and moments of intimacy that quietly unveil the sacred’s slow collapse in modern society. In these images, religion is not displayed—it lingers.

It survives as habit, as an involuntary gesture, as the final refuge in spaces emptied of shared meaning.

The subjects—often elderly, forgotten, alone—seem caught in rituals that no longer offer salvation, only repetition.

Prayer becomes less a conversation with the divine, and more an act of resistance— against noise, against oblivion, against a world that has stopped listening.

The black-and-white aesthetic deepens the absence of a future; each frame becomes a visual relic, a quiet witness to the end of something that may never return.

And yet—within the shadows, in the grain of every detail— a stubborn humanity surfaces, refusing to surrender to the void.

It is within that quiet defiance that the question begins to unfold, not merely of faith, but of the deep, unspoken her power still holds in the hollow spaces we’ve left behind.

title: Portraits of the Master Fulvio Rendhell
text:
Sara Aliscioni’s encounter with Fulvio Rendhell takes place in Sermoneta, a place where history seems to hold on to something indecipherable. Rendhell, a well-known esotericist, scholar of the occult and medium, has devoted much of his life to exploring magic, spiritualism and phenomena that, according to his experience, challenge the boundaries of known reality. Conversations about cosmic light, the origins of existence and the boundary between the visible world and what lies beyond our gaze become the starting point for a photographic project that unfolds inside the Master’s home.

Aliscioni enters his world without attempting to interpret it or uncover its secrets. The photographer observes. She moves through the domestic spaces as a discreet, almost alien presence, recording what unfolds before her lens while leaving untouched what remains incomprehensible. There is no intention to explain, but rather a quiet approach to a private dimension in which everyday life seems to coexist with something that does not entirely belong to reality.

The black-and-white portraits convey this experience through sparse lighting, deep shadows and essential compositions. The house is not merely a physical space, but a place permeated by an invisible tension. The objects, the rooms and Rendhell himself seem to belong to a suspended time, removed from the ordinary rhythm of things. Each image captures a fragment of this atmosphere without offering answers or pointing in any particular direction.

The Master appears within his own dimension, at times absorbed in thought, at others enigmatically present. The camera does not intrude upon his space; it observes him from a distance that preserves the ambiguity of the encounter. Aliscioni does not seek revelation, but records the anticipation of it. It is as though, through the lens, one could approach a threshold without crossing it.

The project thus unfolds as a silent exploration of a personal universe, where light seems to take on a meaning that extends beyond its physical nature. The photographs do more than document a person and his surroundings: they suggest the existence of an uncertain territory, somewhere between what can be seen and what can only be sensed.

The photographer remains an outside observer, a passing witness. She enters, looks and records. Then she allows the images to hold on to the mystery. For not everything we encounter is meant to be understood, and perhaps some places reveal their true nature only to those who know how to remain at the threshold.

title: Portraits
text:
Sara Aliscioni’s portraits emerge from an encounter and from the time it takes for one gaze to draw closer to another. Before photography comes the relationship: a process of getting to know one another and building trust that allows the photographer to enter, at least in part, the world of those she portrays. It is from this closeness that the photographic act takes shape, transforming an encounter into an image of intense presence.

The subjects are portrayed through a rigorous, essential visual language. Their faces, gazes and postures take on a hieratic, almost sculptural quality, suspended between naturalness and stillness. For a moment, the people portrayed seem to withdraw from the flow of everyday life, as though time were slowing down around them. Their presence asserts itself without emphatic gestures, relying instead on the intensity of their gaze, their posture and their relationship with the surrounding space.

Aliscioni’s work reveals echoes of Nordic cinema and the principles of Dogme 95, areas she has explored through dedicated study. Her attention to the subjects’ authentic presence, the reduction of superfluous elements and the rejection of overly contrived imagery evoke a direct approach, in which intensity arises from the situation itself and from the quality of the encounter. Alongside these influences is a more contemplative understanding of time and the image, allowing a silent tension to emerge in the portraits, shaped by anticipation, density and suspension.

Created in a variety of settings, the portraits establish a close relationship between each person and their surroundings. The spaces are not mere backdrops but active elements in the construction of the image, helping to define its atmosphere and convey something of each subject’s individual world. Composition, light and the arrangement of bodies create an essential balance in which every element seems to occupy a necessary place.

Aliscioni does not seek to explain people through photography or reduce them to an immediately recognisable identity. Her gaze remains attentive without becoming intrusive. Even when a portrait appears direct and frontal, a certain distance persists, protecting the subject’s autonomy and preserving their ambiguity. The image does not claim to reveal everything; it leaves room for what cannot be fully known.

The project thus unfolds as a collection of presences, encounters and silences. Each portrait captures a moment in which a person allows themselves to be seen without becoming entirely accessible. Through intense, austere and unembellished images, Sara Aliscioni explores the possibility of portraying others without exhausting their mystery, allowing photography itself to give form to the subtle tension between closeness and distance, reality and perception, presence and absence.

title: Dummies
text:
In Dummies, Aliscioni explores the ambiguous boundary between identity and representation, between body and simulacrum, between presence and absence.

The mannequins become the protagonists of a visual narrative in which the human seems to survive only through its artificial reproduction. Figures devoid of identity, yet charged with an unsettling presence, occupy the space like fragments of a suspended humanity, stripped of their individuality and transformed into images.

They are not merely display objects: they are simulacra, silent doubles of a society that constantly constructs models, images and identities to be worn. Their stillness seems to conceal a deeper tension: the tension between what appears to be and what truly exists.

Through a radical use of black and white, strong contrasts of light and shadow, Aliscioni removes the figures from their original function and draws them into an almost metaphysical dimension. Forms emerge from the darkness, faces multiply and merge, while the plastic material takes on a surprisingly organic quality.

Dummies thus opens up a reflection on the condition of the contemporary individual, the progressive standardisation of bodies, and the fragility of identity within a culture dominated by appearances and reproducibility.

In this suspended universe, the mannequin no longer represents the absence of the human being, but becomes its unsettling mirror. A silent presence in which the viewer may recognise not so much someone else, but a possible image of themselves.

Because, ultimately, when the human becomes representation, where does the model end and its double begin?
